exceedCredits.question: What happens if I run out of credits?
exceedCredits.answer: New runs and conversations are held until you top up, so a runaway job can never quietly bill you. You can raise the credit pack on your current plan with the slider, upgrade, or buy a one-time Pay As You Go top-up ($10 / $50 / $100). PAYG credits stay across renewal cycles and are consumed after your plan credits.

changePlans.question: Can I change plans at any time?
changePlans.answer: Upgrades take effect immediately and are prorated by the payment provider. A downgrade, or a smaller credit pack, is scheduled for the end of the period you already paid for, so you keep what you bought until then. A scheduled change can usually be cancelled before it applies.

payAsYouGo.question: How does Pay As You Go work?
payAsYouGo.answer: Pay As You Go is a one-time top-up: pick $10, $50 or $100 and your wallet is credited with 8,000, 40,000 or 80,000 credits. No subscription required. Those credits stay across renewal cycles and are only spent once your plan credits are gone.

sharedStorage.question: Is storage shared between users?
sharedStorage.answer: Each account has its own storage. Team plans add a shared pool, so a workspace's files count against the team allowance rather than each member's own quota.

conversationCost.question: How many conversations do my credits cover?
conversationCost.answer: You are billed for the tokens a model reads and writes, never per message, so it depends on how much work you ask for. A plain question and answer, with no tool involved, costs about {simpleCredits} credits. A conversation in which an agent builds a workflow for you, around 5 turns and 45 tool calls, costs about {agentCredits}, and a longer build costs proportionally more. A single classification step inside a running workflow is about {classifyCredits}. Priced on a lightweight model such as {basisModel}; a top-tier model costs more.

rollover.question: Do unused credits roll over?
rollover.answer: Plan credits reset at each renewal, so a month's pack is meant to be spent within that month. Pay As You Go top-ups behave differently: they stay in your wallet across renewals and are only used once the month's plan credits are gone.

helloWorkflow.title: Hello workflow
helloWorkflow.description: The smallest workflow that does something: a manual trigger and one step that computes two values.

teaches.0: Every workflow starts with a trigger
teaches.1: How a step reads the output of the step before it
teaches.2: Where to see what a step produced after a run

trigger.label: Start here
trigger.text: A workflow always begins with a trigger. This one is manual: nothing happens until you press Run. Other triggers fire on a webhook, on a schedule, on a new chat message, or when another workflow fails.

label.label: Labels are identifiers
label.text: A step's label is also its name in expressions. 'Build greeting' becomes build_greeting, which is why the connection reads core:build_greeting and the expression above reads trigger:start.output.triggered_by. Rename a step and you must update the expressions that point at it.

output.label: See what a step produced
output.text: Press Run, then click this step. The right panel shows its outputs. A transform puts its mapped fields under transformed, so a later step reads them with {{core:build_greeting.output.transformed.greeting}}. Leave out the transformed segment and the expression resolves to nothing, silently.

branchDecision.title: Branch with a decision
branchDecision.description: A decision sends the run down exactly one path, based on a condition you write.

teaches.0: A decision takes one branch and only one
teaches.1: How to connect a specific port of a decision
teaches.2: Why the branch not taken is marked SKIPPED, not failed

oneBranch.label: One branch, never two
oneBranch.text: A decision evaluates its conditions top to bottom and takes the FIRST one that matches. It never runs two branches. If you want several paths to run at the same time, you want a Fork instead.

ports.label: The port is part of the connection
ports.text: A decision does not just connect to the next step, it connects FROM a specific port. That is why these connections read core:check_amount:if and core:check_amount:else. Extra conditions add elseif_0, then elseif_1, and so on: the elseif ports are numbered from zero, like fork branches.

elseRequired.label: Always keep an else
elseRequired.text: Without an else branch, a value you did not anticipate stops the run on that path: the steps below are marked SKIPPED and no error is raised anywhere. Parallel branches elsewhere keep going. The else branch is where you handle the case you did not think of.

skipped.label: SKIPPED is not a failure
skipped.text: After a run, the branch that was not taken shows as SKIPPED. That is the normal, healthy result of a decision. Only a red FAILED step means something went wrong.

forkMerge.title: Run steps in parallel
forkMerge.description: A fork runs every branch at the same time, and a merge waits until all of them are done.

teaches.0: A fork runs all of its branches, unlike a decision
teaches.1: A merge waits for every predecessor before continuing
teaches.2: Any step with several incoming connections already merges

vsDecision.label: Fork is not decision
vsDecision.text: A decision picks ONE branch. A fork runs them ALL, at the same time. Use a fork when the branches are independent and you want the run to be faster.

allBranches.label: All branches start together
allBranches.text: Both branches below start at the same moment. Their ports are numbered from zero: core:fan_out:branch_0 and core:fan_out:branch_1.

waitsAll.label: The merge waits for everyone
waitsAll.text: Join does not run until BOTH branches have finished. Finished means completed, failed OR skipped: a branch that failed still releases the merge, which is exactly what lets a resilient step carry the run forward instead of hanging it.

implicitMerge.label: Merges can be implicit
implicitMerge.text: Any step with more than one incoming connection already behaves like a merge: it waits for all of its predecessors. The Merge step exists for when you want that wait to be visible and named on the canvas, not because it is required.

splitList.title: Process a list
splitList.description: A split turns one list into many parallel runs, one per item, then an aggregate collects the results.

teaches.0: A split creates one parallel context per item
teaches.1: How to read the current item with {{item}} and {{index}}
teaches.2: The difference between a split and a loop

parallel.label: One run per item
parallel.text: Split takes a list and starts the steps after it once per item, in parallel. Three items means the steps below run three times, at the same time, each with its own item.

vsLoop.label: Split is not loop
vsLoop.text: Split runs N copies in parallel over the items of a list. Loop repeats sequentially, one pass after another, for as long as a condition stays true. Use split for a known list, loop for a condition you have to re-check.

itemVar.label: Reading the current item
itemVar.text: Inside the split, {{item}} is the current element and {{index}} is its position, starting at zero. They resolve for every step of the per-item region, including a decision or a loop, which simply run once per item. The region ends at the step that folds the items back into one: an aggregate, or a merge that gathers the split.

maxItems.label: maxItems is a safety net
maxItems.text: maxItems caps how many items the split will take, here 10 (the default is 100). Read this one carefully: items beyond the cap are DROPPED silently, with no error and nothing in the run to tell you. Set it above the largest list you realistically expect, it is a safety net against a runaway list, not a performance dial.

aggregate.label: Collecting the results back
aggregate.text: The parallel branches end here. Aggregate gathers one value from each of them into a single list, which is how you get back to a single execution after a split.

resilientSteps.title: Make a step resilient
resilientSteps.description: Retries, timeouts and an explicit failure step, so a flaky call does not silently break the whole run.

teaches.0: How retries, backoff and timeout are configured per step
teaches.2: How to fail the run on purpose, with a clear message

replaceUrl.label: Replace the URL first
replaceUrl.text: This step points at a placeholder address. Open it and set your own URL before you run this workflow, otherwise the call fails by design.

retry.label: Retries and backoff
retry.text: retryCount is 2, which means 3 attempts in total: the first one plus 2 retries. retryBackoffMs waits 1000 ms between attempts. One thing to understand before you rely on this: an HTTP 4xx or 5xx response is NOT a step failure, the step succeeds with success set to false. Retries only fire on a hard failure such as an unreachable host, a timeout, or an invalid URL. Everything else is handled by the decision opposite.

timeout.label: A timeout stops waiting, not the work
timeout.text: Two timeouts are in play here and they are independent. The HTTP step has its own transport timeout (5000 ms), while nodePolicy.timeoutMs (15000 ms) caps each attempt of the call itself. Keep the step-level one above the transport one, otherwise the wrapper fires first and hides the real error. And be careful what a timeout means: you stop WAITING for the answer, but the remote server may well have received and processed your request. For anything that writes data, make the call safe to repeat.

continueOnFailure.label: continueOnFailure keeps the run alive
continueOnFailure.text: Without it, a failed step marks everything after it as skipped. With it, the run carries on, though the step itself still shows as FAILED. On a hard failure the step does NOT produce the fields you expected (success and data are absent), so an expression pointing at them resolves to nothing and the decision below falls through to else. continueOnFailure is refused on a decision, a switch or an option: a branching step that failed chose no port.

stopOnError.label: Failing on purpose
stopOnError.text: Stop on Error ends the ENTIRE run, every branch, and marks it FAILED with the message you wrote. Prefer it to letting a run finish green on bad data: a loud failure is easier to fix than a silent one.

resilientSteps.stopMessage: The API call failed after every retry attempt.

errorHandler.title: React to a failure
errorHandler.description: Two workflows side by side: one that fails, and one that wakes up when it does.

teaches.0: How an error trigger watches a parent workflow
teaches.2: The one setup step everyone forgets

pickParent.label: Choose the workflow to watch
pickParent.text: Both halves are drawn on one canvas so the shape is easy to read, but they CANNOT stay together. A workflow that contains an error trigger never dispatches its own failures (that is the anti-loop guard), so this handler will never react to the run above it. Move the top DAG into its own workflow, then add a fresh Error trigger here from the palette and pick that workflow as the parent. The watched workflow cannot be changed from the inspector afterwards.

seedRun.label: Run this workflow once, or it stays deaf
seedRun.text: This is the step almost everyone misses. Save this workflow, then run it manually one time, and leave that run in progress. A handler is only reached through a run that is already waiting: if none exists, failures of the parent are ignored SILENTLY, with no error, no warning, and nothing in the parent run to tell you the handler never fired.

payload.label: What you receive
payload.text: The trigger hands you status (the parent run state at the moment it was dispatched, not always FAILED), parentWorkflowId, parentRunId, errorMessage and triggeredAt, plus the counts failedSteps, completedSteps, totalSteps and skippedSteps when the parent reported statistics. The step next to this note copies a few of them so you can see their shape after a run.

noLoop.label: No infinite loops
noLoop.text: An error handler that fails does not trigger another error handler. You cannot accidentally build a chain of failures that feeds itself.

nextStep.label: Where to go from here
nextStep.text: The top DAG is only a stand-in for the workflow you actually want to watch: it does a little work, then fails on purpose. The bottom DAG is the handler. Replace both with the real thing once the shape is clear.

errorHandler.stopMessage: Failing on purpose, so the handler beside this has something to react to.

interfacePage.title: Show a page to the user
interfacePage.description: A workflow that builds some data and hands it to a web page, then waits for the user to continue.

teaches.0: The workflow is the backend, the interface is the frontend
teaches.1: How variable_mapping feeds values into the page
teaches.2: Why the run pauses at an interface until the user acts

interfacePage.interfaceDescription: Result page created from the "Show a page to the user" template.

backendFrontend.label: Two halves of one app
backendFrontend.text: Think of it this way: the workflow is the backend and the interface is the frontend. Steps compute values, the page displays them. The page never queries the database itself, everything it shows arrives from the workflow.

variableMapping.label: How values reach the page
variableMapping.text: The interface node carries a variable_mapping: each entry names a placeholder in the HTML and the expression that fills it. Here headline, who and when come from the transform before it, and the page writes them as {{headline}}, {{who}} and {{when}}. The |default part after a pipe is what shows when a value is missing.

pauses.label: The run stops here, on purpose
pauses.text: An interface step waits. The run holds at this node until the user acts, which is what makes multi-step apps possible. The button on the page sends __continue, the one action that advances the workflow. A plain navigate action would switch pages without advancing it.

ownCopy.label: This page is yours now
ownCopy.text: Creating from this template also created a real interface, owned by you and listed under Interfaces. Edit its HTML and CSS freely: you are changing your own copy, never the template.

page.headline: Your workflow built this page
page.hint: Every value on this page came from the step before it. Change that step, run again, and the page changes with it.

basicAssistant.title: Basic assistant
basicAssistant.description: A plain conversational agent with no tools, and a system prompt written as a worked example.

teaches.0: The four parts of a system prompt that works
teaches.1: Why an agent with no tools is a fine starting point

basicAssistant.systemPrompt:
You are a helpful assistant for a small team.

Role: you answer questions clearly and briefly, and you help people think through problems.

Tone: direct and friendly. Short sentences. No filler, no flattery.

Rules:
- If you do not know something, say so instead of guessing.
- Ask a clarifying question when the request is ambiguous.
- Never invent facts, names, numbers or sources.

Format: answer in plain prose. Use a short bulleted list only when you are genuinely enumerating things.

(This prompt is a starting point. The four blocks above, role, tone, rules and format, are the parts worth keeping when you rewrite it for your own use.)

dataAnalyst.title: Data analyst
dataAnalyst.description: An agent that can read your tables, in read-only mode, and is told to always say where a number came from.

teaches.0: How to grant an agent access to one family of resources
teaches.1: Why read-only access is the right default
teaches.2: Asking an agent to cite its source

dataAnalyst.systemPrompt:
You are a data analyst working with the team's tables.

Role: answer questions about the data by reading the tables you have access to.

Rules:
- Always read the data before answering. Never estimate a number from memory.
- State which table and which columns a figure came from, every time.
- If the tables do not contain the answer, say exactly that, and say what would be needed.
- If a result looks surprising, show the figure and flag it rather than smoothing it over.

Format: give the number first, then a one-line explanation of how you got it. Use a small table when comparing several values.

You have READ access only. You cannot modify the data, and you should not offer to.

workflowConductor.title: Workflow conductor
workflowConductor.description: An agent allowed to run your workflows, with clear instructions about when it should and should not.

teaches.0: An agent can trigger the workflows you built
teaches.1: How to frame when an agent may act instead of answer
teaches.2: Why you tell an agent to confirm before side effects

workflowConductor.systemPrompt:
You coordinate the team's workflows.

Role: understand what the user is asking for, decide whether an existing workflow does it, and run that workflow.

Rules:
- Before running anything, say which workflow you intend to run and why.
- Ask for confirmation before any workflow that sends a message, writes data, or is otherwise visible outside this conversation.
- If no workflow matches the request, say so. Do not improvise a substitute.
- After a run, report what happened: succeeded, failed, or partially, and what the output was.

Format: keep it short. One line for the intent, one line for the result.

frugalAgent.title: Frugal agent
frugalAgent.description: Tight limits and a zero temperature, for repetitive work where cost and consistency matter more than flair.

teaches.0: maxIterations caps how many turns an agent can take
teaches.1: maxTokens caps the length of each answer
teaches.2: Temperature zero makes the same input give the same output

frugalAgent.systemPrompt:
You perform short, repetitive tasks with a predictable output.

Role: do exactly what is asked, once, and stop.

Rules:
- Be brief. No preamble, no summary of the request, no closing pleasantries.
- Do not ask follow-up questions unless the task is impossible without one.
- Give the same answer for the same input. Do not vary the wording for style.
- If the task needs more steps than you are allowed, say what is missing and stop.

Format: output only the result. No explanation unless it was requested.

(Cost levers live in the Advanced section: maxIterations limits how many turns this agent may take, maxTokens limits the size of each answer, and a credit budget stops it entirely once spent.)

faq.title: Frequently asked questions

what.question: What is LiveContext?
what.answer: LiveContext is an AI automation platform. You describe a job in chat, the workflow builds itself in front of you, AI agents run it with scoped tool access and hard credit budgets, and the result ships as an app your team or customers can use. It includes {integrations} API integrations, built-in data tables, a browser-use agent and a marketplace of forkable automations.

code.question: Do I need to know how to code?
code.answer: No. You build by describing the job in chat and refining on a visual canvas. When you want them, power tools are there: a code node, raw HTTP requests, database queries and custom API definitions.

selfHost.question: Can I self-host LiveContext?
selfHost.answer: Yes. The Community Edition is free and self-hosted: one docker compose up on your own server, with the code public on GitHub. The cloud edition adds managed hosting, SAML SSO, workspaces and platform credits.

compare.question: How is LiveContext different from Zapier, n8n or Make?
compare.answer: Those tools focus on the pipeline; LiveContext covers the whole loop: the chat that builds the workflow, the agents that run it under budgets and scoped access, the app your team opens, and the tables that hold the data. See the detailed comparisons at livecontext.ai/compare.

pricing.question: How does pricing work?
pricing.answer: There is a free tier with no credit card required. Paid plans are credit-based: you pick a credit tier and can cap the spend per agent with a hard budget it cannot exceed. The self-hosted Community Edition is free.

models.question: Which AI models can I use?
models.answer: Major providers are supported, including Anthropic Claude, OpenAI up to GPT-6 Astra, Google Gemini and DeepSeek, plus Jev, TypeSafe's decision model for classification steps. Use platform credits or bring your own API keys, and pick the model per agent.

telegram.1: In Telegram, open @BotFather, send /newbot and copy the token it gives you.
telegram.3: Open your bot and press Start (for a group: add the bot to the group and send a message there). A bot cannot write to someone who never wrote to it.
telegram.4: Give the chat to write to: for yourself, your numeric id, which @userinfobot sends you when you write to it.

slack.1: Connect Slack below and approve the app in your workspace.
slack.2: For a channel, type /invite followed by the app name in it. A direct message needs nothing.
slack.3: Pick the channel or conversation with Find my chats.

discord.1: In the Discord Developer Portal, create an application, open Bot and copy its token.
discord.2: In OAuth2, URL Generator, tick bot and Send Messages, open the link and add the bot to your server.
discord.3: Paste the token below, and the Public Key (General Information page) in the field under it.
discord.4: Pick the channel, then paste the Interactions Endpoint URL shown after connecting on the General Information page.

whatsapp.1: In your Meta app with WhatsApp, API Setup: note the Phone number ID and create a permanent System User token.
whatsapp.2: Paste the token below, and the Phone number ID in the field under it.
whatsapp.3: From the phone that will answer, send any message to your business number (WhatsApp only allows a reply within 24 hours).
whatsapp.4: Type that phone number, then set the callback URL and verify token shown after connecting.

teams.2: Pick the chat with Find my chats.
teams.3: Messages are posted as you, and Teams does not notify you about your own messages: pick a chat others read, or another service to be notified yourself.
